pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–13 years

- **Topic:** Reactions That Release or Absorb Heat (Energetics)

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Energetics):** pupils are taught "energy changes on changes of state (qualitative)" and "exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative)," i.e. that some reactions give out energy to the surroundings (temperature rises) and others take energy in (temperature falls).

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-6):** undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes — an explicit application of exothermic and endothermic reactions.

- **Operational details:** Teach energetics operationally through temperature change: an exothermic reaction transfers energy OUT, so the surroundings (and thermometer) get warmer (combustion, neutralisation, most oxidation, hand-warmers); an endothermic reaction takes energy IN, so the surroundings get colder (thermal decomposition, dissolving certain salts, the citric acid + sodium bicarbonate sherbet reaction, instant cold packs). Keep it qualitative at KS3 — measure the temperature before and after and classify by the direction of change; do NOT introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy calculations or reaction profiles with numbers (those are KS4/GCSE). The productive idea is that chemical reactions always involve an energy transfer with the surroundings, and 'feels hot' vs 'feels cold' is the everyday signature of which way energy flowed.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Given a reaction's temperature change, the child classifies it as exothermic or endothermic and states the direction of energy transfer between reaction and surroundings.
bestPractices: Define exothermic and endothermic by the DIRECTION of energy transfer with the surroundings, using the thermometer reading as the operational signature (up = out, down = in).
Have pupils measure temperature before and after and classify from their own data rather than being told which reactions are which.
Include at least one surprising endothermic example (dissolving ammonium nitrate, sherbet) so pupils don't assume all reactions release heat.
Keep it strictly qualitative at KS3 — direction of change only; defer enthalpy values, reaction profiles and bond-energy sums to KS4.
Link to everyday devices (hand-warmers, instant cold packs) so the abstract energy transfer is grounded in real products.
keyRepresentations: A thermometer / temperature–time graph rising (exothermic) or falling (endothermic).
Energy-flow arrows pointing OUT of the reaction (exo) or IN from the surroundings (endo).
Paired beakers: one warming, one cooling.
Everyday device cards: hand-warmer (exo) vs instant cold pack (endo).
A two-bin sort (exothermic / endothermic) of reactions and scenarios.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming all chemical reactions give out heat, missing that some absorb it and cool the surroundings.
Reversing the terms — thinking 'exothermic' means it gets colder because energy 'exits'.
Believing 'endothermic' reactions produce cold as a substance rather than absorbing energy from the surroundings.
Confusing the reaction system with the surroundings when deciding which way energy flowed.
Thinking heating is always needed for a reaction to occur, conflating 'needs heat to start' with 'absorbs heat overall'.

learn.summary: For ages 12–13 (UK KS3, US NGSS MS-PS1-6), teach exothermic and endothermic processes operationally through the direction of temperature change: temperature up means energy transferred OUT to the surroundings (exothermic); temperature down means energy transferred IN from the surroundings (endothermic). Keep it strictly qualitative at this level — classify from measured temperature change, do not introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy sums or numerical reaction profiles. The central activity is measuring temperature before and after several reactions (and physical changes such as dissolving) and classifying each from the pupil's own data, deliberately including a surprising endothermic case so pupils don't assume all reactions release heat. An optional NGSS design extension and everyday-example matching reinforce the idea.

activities.title: Measure, graph and classify: a temperature-change bench
feedback: If a pupil assumes every reaction warms the cup, point them back to the ammonium-nitrate run where the temperature fell — this directly challenges the 'all reactions give out heat' assumption.

If a pupil says the cup got cold because 'cold got in', recast: there is only thermal energy moving; here the process absorbed energy FROM the water, so the water has less thermal energy and reads colder. 'Cold' just means a lower temperature (less thermal energy); it is not a substance arriving.

If a pupil reverses the terms, pin the convention to the surroundings: exo = energy EXits to surroundings (they warm); endo = energy ENters the reaction from surroundings (they cool). Re-classify several runs by their temperature change.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'You classified it from the direction the temperature moved, not from what the reaction looks like — that's exactly the signature of energy transfer.'
activities.rationale: The concept is a measured change over time, so pupils classifying from their own temperature data (rather than being told which case is which) connects the term to the observed direction of energy flow. A deliberately surprising endothermic case targets the common misconception that all reactions release heat. A live thermometer, a temperature–time trace, and energy-flow arrows (OUT for exo, IN for endo) are optional representations that make the energy-transfer direction concrete; a real cup-and-thermometer practical is an equally valid form of this activity.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative) and energy changes on changes of state (qualitative).
learnerActions: Choose a reaction or dissolving process (e.g. acid + alkali neutralisation, a combustion example, dissolving ammonium nitrate, or citric acid + sodium bicarbonate) and record the starting temperature. Note that dissolving is a physical change, but it still involves an energy transfer with the surroundings.

Begin the reaction or dissolving process (e.g. pour the reactants together, or stir the salt into water; a combustion example would be run as a demonstration rather than mixed in a cup) and watch the thermometer, recording temperature over time to produce a temperature–time trace.
Decide from the direction of change whether energy flowed OUT to the surroundings (temperature rose, exothermic) or IN from the surroundings (temperature fell, endothermic).
Run at least one case you expect to warm and one that unexpectedly cools (dissolving ammonium nitrate, or the sherbet reaction), and compare.
Sort each result into an 'exothermic' or 'endothermic' bin and state the rule you discovered: temperature up = energy out; temperature down = energy in.
activities.intendedInsight: Every chemical reaction — and many physical changes such as dissolving — involves an energy transfer with its surroundings, and the thermometer reading is the everyday signature of which way energy flowed. 'Mixing chemicals' can make things colder as well as hotter, because energy can be absorbed from the surroundings.

activities.title: Design a hand-warmer or cold pack to a target temperature
feedback: If the pupil picks a warming process for a cold pack, ask which way energy must flow relative to the hand for it to feel cold, and revisit the exo/endo direction.

Reinforce measurement: if the pupil's data show that changing the amount of substance (with the same amount of water) changed the temperature reached, say: 'You adjusted the amount and the temperature changed — you're controlling the size of the energy transfer, still qualitatively at this stage.'
activities.rationale: NGSS MS-PS1-6 frames energetics as a design task: construct, test and modify a device that releases or absorbs thermal energy. This is proposed to ground the abstract energy-transfer idea in a real, buildable product and asks for construction and explanation as well as recognition; its efficacy is intended rather than independently verified here.
sourceClaims: Students undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes.
learnerActions: Pick a goal: a device that gets warm (hand-warmer) or one that gets cold (instant cold pack).
Decide whether you need an exothermic or endothermic process to reach that goal, explaining the direction of energy transfer.
Assemble, test and measure the temperature your device reaches, then modify it to get closer to a target temperature.
Explain in terms of energy transfer with the surroundings why your device feels hot or cold.
activities.intendedInsight: Exothermic and endothermic processes are the basis of real devices; choosing the right direction of energy transfer lets you engineer a warming or cooling effect.

activities.title: Energy changes in changes of state, and conservation
feedback: If a pupil restricts energy changes to burning, show that melting absorbs energy (endothermic) and freezing releases it (exothermic), and dissolving can go either way.
If a pupil says cold flowed in, redirect to conservation: if the water cooled, the dissolving/reacting substance absorbed that energy — ask them to name where the energy went.
activities.rationale: The assessment evidence requires explaining energy changes during changes of state (melting endothermic, freezing exothermic) and tying classification to conservation of energy. This addresses the misconception that only 'burning-type' reactions involve energy changes and the 'cold is a substance' idea.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught exothermic and endothermic chemical reactions (qualitative) and energy changes on changes of state (qualitative).
learnerActions: Classify melting ice and freezing water as endothermic or exothermic, justifying each by whether energy is absorbed from or released to the surroundings.
Explain how a cold pack that cools works even though 'nothing cold' was added.
State what gained the energy when the water in a cold pack cooled, using the idea that total energy is conserved.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy changes accompany physical changes (melting, freezing, dissolving) as well as dramatic reactions, and because energy is conserved, cooling means energy was transferred from the water to the dissolving/reacting system, not that 'cold' arrived.

activities.title: Sort reactions, changes and everyday devices by energy direction
feedback: For a correct sort, prompt the pupil to state the reasoning: 'You put the cold pack with endothermic because it absorbs energy from your hand.'
For an error, return to the rule temperature up = energy out, temperature down = energy in, and have them re-check against it.

For the thermal decompositions usually met at this level (e.g. heating calcium carbonate or copper carbonate), remind pupils they are endothermic because energy must be supplied continuously: stop heating and the decomposition stops. This is different from a reaction that only needs heat to start and then keeps going by releasing energy (exothermic), such as combustion. A few decompositions are exothermic, so judge each by the direction of energy transfer during the change.
For photosynthesis, note it is endothermic because it absorbs light energy; classify it by energy taken in, not by a temperature reading.
activities.rationale: Categorisation and matching consolidate and let pupils check their classification across many cases, including the everyday examples that ground the abstract idea. A sort or match can check and reinforce classification but does not by itself elicit the measure-and-classify-from-own-data experience; it is a consolidation and checking activity, not the primary learning experience.
learnerActions: Sort given items — reactions, physical changes and scenarios (combustion, neutralisation, dissolving ammonium nitrate, sherbet, thermal decomposition, photosynthesis) — into exothermic and endothermic groups.
Match everyday products — hand-warmer, instant cold pack, campfire — to exothermic or endothermic, and say which way energy flows relative to you.
For a stated temperature change (e.g. 'the temperature fell'), state whether energy was absorbed or released, and predict whether a thermometer will end higher or lower.
activities.intendedInsight: The same classification rule applies across reactions, physical changes and real devices: match the direction of temperature change to the direction of energy transfer.

constraints: Keep strictly qualitative at this level: classify by the direction of energy transfer, usually shown by the direction of temperature change in the surroundings. For cases where no simple temperature reading applies (e.g. photosynthesis absorbing light, or a decomposition that needs continuous heating), classify by whether energy is taken in or given out. Do not introduce enthalpy values, bond-energy calculations, or numerical reaction profiles (those belong to KS4/GCSE).

Sorting, matching and multiple-choice tasks consolidate and check classification but do not by themselves elicit the measure-and-classify-from-own-data experience; use them alongside, not instead of, an experiment or temperature-trace activity.

A static tappable diagram (e.g. one warming beaker and one cooling beaker with arrows in/out) is a useful vocabulary anchor for exo/endo but a fixed reveal cannot let pupils generate and classify their own temperature data; treat it as a scaffold.
Address 'cold is a substance' language directly: there is only thermal energy moving; cooling means energy was absorbed from the surroundings, not that cold arrived.
Pin the exo/endo convention to the surroundings to prevent reversal: exo = energy exits to the surroundings (they warm); endo = energy enters the reaction from the surroundings (they cool).
Include at least one surprising endothermic example so pupils do not assume all reactions release heat.
Distinguish 'needs heat to start' from 'absorbs heat overall' — a reaction that must be heated to begin can still be exothermic.

Treat dissolving, melting and freezing as physical changes that still involve energy transfer; do not label dissolving as a chemical reaction, even though it can be classified exo/endo by the same temperature-direction rule.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS MS-PS1-6 design-project source claim is marked verified:false in the original row; treat the design extension as consistent with that standard but not independently confirmed here, and read efficacy wording as proposed/intended.

The original rated 3D and open-conversation formats 'poor' with claims such as '3D adds no insight' and 'dialogue cannot substitute' for measuring. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the source evidence; they have been softened to the scoped point that the core learning depends on generating and classifying temperature data, which a tappable diagram or discussion alone does not itself provide. No universal 'only this teaches' claim is asserted.

The original (and the first-draft candidate) loosely called dissolving ammonium nitrate 'a reaction'. Dissolving is a physical change; this has been corrected in every learner-facing occurrence to 'reaction or dissolving process', consistent with the changes-of-state evidence. This is a wording correction, not new source verification.
Photosynthesis (endothermic) was named in the original evidence and had been dropped; it has been restored as an endothermic example in the sort activity.

Self-audit of science content: the state-change classifications (melting endothermic, freezing exothermic), the exo/endo direction convention, thermal decomposition as endothermic, and photosynthesis as endothermic are internally consistent and were preserved. The 'cold is a substance' correction is retained as a conceptual fix, not new verification.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: put a thermometer in water and stir in ammonium nitrate. Ask the child to predict whether the temperature rises, falls, or stays the same, and WHY, before adding it. A 'reactions give out heat' or 'nothing cold added' model predicts a rise or no change. The temperature drops sharply. The pre-observation reasoning about energy direction is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If no 'cold' entered the water, where did the water's energy GO?
A hand warmer gets hot; a cold pack gets cold. Which way is energy flowing in each, relative to your hand?
Is melting ice exothermic or endothermic — and how does that fit the cold-pack case?
Overall energy is conserved. So in the cold pack, if the water cooled, what gained that energy?
assess.correctAnswer: No cold 'gets in' — there is no such thing as cold flowing in. This is an ENDOTHERMIC change: the dissolving/reaction ABSORBS thermal energy FROM the water and surroundings, so their temperature drops. Cold is the absence of energy that has been taken away, not a substance arriving. Full marks explain the temperature fall as energy being absorbed BY the system from the surroundings.

errorPatterns.pattern: cold is a substance/thing that flows into objects to cool them ('coldness went into the water')
errorPatterns.nextMove: There is only thermal energy moving; 'cold' is where energy has been removed. Recast: the reaction absorbs energy from the water, so the water has less → colder. Confront the 'cold substance' idea directly.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — coldness from the powder moves into the water and cools it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: explains cooling by cold entering rather than heat energy leaving/being absorbed

errorPatterns.nextMove: Pin the convention to the surroundings: exo = energy EXits to surroundings, they warm; endo = energy ENters the reaction from surroundings, they cool. Re-classify several by the temperature change.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's exothermic, because a reaction always gives out energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels a warming reaction endothermic and a cooling one exothermic

errorPatterns.pattern: only 'burning-type' reactions involve energy changes; dissolving/state changes don't
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show melting is endothermic and freezing exothermic, and dissolving can be either — energy changes accompany physical changes too, not just dramatic reactions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies that dissolving or melting has an energy change; restricts exo/endo to combustion

responseLevels.gap: Explains cooling by 'cold flowing in'; reverses exo/endo; thinks only burning has energy changes.
responseLevels.full: Explains temperature change purely as energy transferred to/from the surroundings (no 'cold' substance), classifies reactions and state changes as exo/endo by direction of energy flow, and ties it to conservation of energy — transferring to hand warmers, cold packs, melting and freezing.
responseLevels.partial: Labels a reaction exo/endo from its temperature change and defines the terms, but slips into 'cold as a substance' language or can't apply the idea to state changes — labels without consistent energy-transfer reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I dissolve a spoon of ammonium nitrate in water in a cup and the cup goes noticeably COLD — this is how instant cold packs work. A student says 'something cold must be getting into the water to cool it down.' Is that what's happening — and the important part, explain in terms of energy why the cup gets cold.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who reasons with energy transfer (endothermic = energy absorbed from surroundings, so they cool) from one holding the 'cold is a substance that flows in' misconception. It also tests the direction convention (exothermic releases/warms, endothermic absorbs/cools) rather than rote labels.
